content: In settings with lower prevalence of syphilis, the difference in overtreatment between the single on-site rapid syphilis test (RST, Strategy A) and the single on-site rapid plasma reagin (RPR, Strategy B) test is minimal, with approximately 9 more cases of overtreatment per 1,000 pregnant women using the RPR strategy. However, in higher prevalence settings, the difference in overtreatment becomes more pronounced, favoring the RST strategy, with approximately 30–50 fewer cases of overtreatment per 1,000 pregnant women compared to the RPR strategy. The difference in overtreatment between the combined strategy of on-site RST followed by RPR (Strategy C) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) is negligible. The harms associated with missed treatment are relatively small between the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) in lower prevalence settings, with approximately 4 more missed cases per 1,000 pregnant women using the RPR strategy. However, in higher prevalence settings, the difference becomes moderate, with 25–30 more missed cases per 1,000 pregnant women using the RPR strategy. The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher or similar with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) compared to other strategies, and this trend is consistent across different prevalence settings. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of prioritizing the detection of missed syphilis cases due to the severe adverse effects of syphilis during pregnancy, including the risks of congenital syphilis and fetal death. While overtreatment may result in minor side effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms, and is more likely in women with higher antibody titers due to the sensitivity of the tests, some degree of overtreatment is considered acceptable. However, overtreatment in large proportions of tested women is deemed undesirable. Although there is no direct evidence on the impact of different screening and treatment strategies on partner notification, the GDG agreed that a sequential testing approach (Strategy C) could potentially increase partner treatment. This is because additional confirmatory tests may enhance the confidence of pregnant women and their partners in the positive test results. The cost-effectiveness model demonstrated that the total costs per 1,000 women screened were lowest with the RPR strategy in Tanzania and Zambia. In contrast, in Peru, the use of RSTs was the most cost-effective due to labor costs associated with RPR testing. Overall, the most cost-effective approach across all prevalence settings was the single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A). However, this strategy may incur higher costs in certain settings. Although no studies directly assessed the impact of different strategies on equity, it was noted that some pregnant women in certain countries may face direct costs for screening and/or treatment services. Nevertheless, screening rates achieved with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) appear to be slightly higher, regardless of cost, suggesting that such costs may not significantly reduce equity. There is no evidence comparing the acceptability of RST to RPR. However, studies have shown that both health workers and pregnant women are satisfied with RSTs, as they reduce clinic visits and are easy to use. A systematic review and six studies addressed the feasibility of on-site tests, noting that sequential on-site testing may be unaffordable in some settings and requires adequate provider training. Despite this, on-site tests have been successfully implemented in many countries. The GDG concluded that using a single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A) or a sequential strategy involving RST followed by a first dose of treatment if positive, and then RPR testing with additional doses of treatment if RPR is also positive (Strategy C), may result in a greater number of people treated, fewer missed cases, and fewer incidents of overtreatment compared to other strategies (e.g., Strategy B). In lower prevalence settings, the single on-site RST (Strategy A) or sequential testing and treatment (Strategy C) yielded similar results. However, in higher prevalence settings, fewer pregnant women were overtreated when using the sequential testing and treatment strategy (Strategy C). The single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) is cost-effective, feasible to implement, and acceptable to key stakeholders. Healthcare providers should receive training and information about the prevalence of syphilis in pregnant women and the risks of mother-to-child transmission. Pregnant women and their partners may require additional support when discussing partner treatment. Further research is needed to compare the sensitivity and specificity of sequential testing strategies, as well as to assess important outcomes such as partner notification and treatment, and the long-term consequences of screening and treatment in mothers and infants.
